blocks.text: Accordingly, the sacred doctors refer only hesitantly to the halcyon what they had read in the Greek version about the Sirens; and Chrysostom and Cyril add that others understand τὴν γλαῦκα [tēn glauka], that is, the little owl, and that this is κατὰ τὴν Ἑβραίων ἔκδοσιν [kata tēn Hebraiōn ekdosin], according to the Hebrews' edition, as if the Hebrew word בת־יענה bath-jaana meant this. From this opinion the more recent scholars depart little, namely Pagninus, Arias, Junius and Tremellius, Schindlerus, Buxtorf, and the translators of the vernacular Bibles; [II, 815] for them bath-jaana is the owl or the eagle owl ^{(1)}. And a learned man of our century defends this rendering at length, namely Fuller, in book 6, chapter 7 of his Miscellanea: A kind of bird of this sort, which is both θρηνητικὸν [thrēnētikon] and φιλέρημον [philerēmon], Tremellius rightly, I think, renders owl, which the Greeks (as also the Latins) call ὀλολυγόνα [ololygona] from its mournful, as it were, howling. In the same way they named it יענה jaana from ענה, to cry out or resound, namely because of its sonorous voice, especially in the silence of the night, and often repeated. Unless we prefer (which I rather believe) that it is a certain species of owl which they called the strix. For strix is rendered ὀλολυγὼν [ololygōn] in Greek in an ancient Glossary. Aratus calls it ἐρημαίην [erēmaiēn], that is, a lover of solitude; and it is agreed that its cries were always considered sad and deathly.
